claims.speaker: Chris Wright, U.S. Energy Secretary
claims.quote: Nearly 9 million barrels per day leaving through Hormuz, as a seven-day average.
claims.note: Also reported by Reuters commentary of 2026-08-24.

claims.speaker: Chris Wright, U.S. Energy Secretary
claims.quote: About 15 million barrels per day of total regional flow: roughly 9 through Hormuz plus 5-7 via bypass pipelines and export routes.
claims.note: Not a Hormuz-only figure; includes bypass routes.

claims.speaker: U.S. administration
claims.quote: A claimed 15 million barrels moved on one particular day.
claims.note: Exceptional single-day volume claim, not an average rate.

claims.speaker: U.S. officials
claims.quote: About 10 million barrels per day exiting via the strait itself.
claims.note: Axios described this as roughly half of prewar Hormuz volume.

claims.speaker: U.S. officials
claims.quote: 15 to 20 tankers entering and exiting each night in the U.S.-protected corridor.
claims.note: Inbound plus outbound combined; not equivalent to loaded outbound tankers.

claims.speaker: Chris Wright, U.S. Energy Secretary
claims.quote: An average of about 8 million barrels of oil per day had left Hormuz over the prior seven days.
claims.note: Later reading of the same seven-day series as c1; different windows, not a correction.

claims.speaker: Donald Trump, U.S. President
claims.quote: A graphic posted with 'Hormuz Oil Volumes are BACK' showing about 18 million barrels a day the previous week.
claims.note: Figure read from a posted graphic labelled as the previous week; the chart's source was not stated. Archive USOF-20260903-02.

claims.speaker: Chris Wright, U.S. Energy Secretary
claims.quote: The data as of this morning were at the highest since the start of the conflict, just under 11 million barrels a day, seven-day average of oil and oil products going out of the Strait on ship on water.
claims.note: Bloomberg TV interview, reported by TASS (published 22:57 UTC on 9 September, dateline 10 September). 'Just under 11' recorded as 11.0, as 'nearly 9' is for c1. Oil and oil products, so all liquids: out of the crude episode. A further 3 to 5 million barrels a day through bypass pipelines is a separate figure (archive USOF-20260909-02). Archive USOF-20260909-01.

claims.speaker: Chris Wright, U.S. Energy Secretary
claims.quote: Transit through Hormuz had supplied an average of 10 million barrels per day of crude and oil products.
claims.note: Later reading of the seven-day series as c1 and c6; different windows, not a correction. Crude and products together. Archive USOF-20260913-01.

claims.speaker: Chris Wright, U.S. Energy Secretary
claims.quote: The running average of oil flowing out of the strait was almost 13 million barrels a day.

claims.speaker: Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury Secretary
claims.quote: Excluding Iranian oil, flows through the strait were averaging 15 to 22 million barrels a day.
claims.note: Excludes Iranian oil; window unstated. Archive USOF-20260927-04.

claims.speaker: Chris Wright, U.S. Energy Secretary
claims.quote: Up to 14 million barrels of oil a day moving through the Strait of Hormuz, with flows at 80 to 90 percent of pre-conflict levels.
claims.note: Remarks at the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh. Window unstated. Archive USOF-20261012-02.

estimates.note: Range across commercial trackers; Persian Gulf loadings and subsequent deliveries not corroborating the full U.S. figure.

'Total oil exports from Gulf countries in August are currently estimated around 13 mb/d, nearly half their pre-war level', published 11 September 2026. An intergovernmental agency's estimate, entered as a government estimate for want of a closer type. All liquids and regional, so it never enters the crude episode.
August average for the same seven-country crude and condensate series as e19, published 6 October. Includes Iran and all routes.
Estimate explicitly attempts to include dark transits and ship-to-ship transfers.

'About 6 million to 8 million barrels a day of crude is transiting the strait, traders told Bloomberg this week.' Primary: Bloomberg, Aug 27 2026, 'Hormuz Oil Shipments Rise as Gulf Producers Boost Exports' (traders involved in and monitoring cargo activity; Iraq, Qatar and Kuwait barrels seen in Bloomberg/Kpler/Vortexa vessel data). First independent figure whose upper end reaches the administration range (8-10); sits above the tracker consensus (~5) and the WSJ tracker range (2-6). Anonymous market participants, not a model.

Named-tracker figure distinct from e1 (anonymous 'vessel-monitoring services consensus,' Reuters, Aug. 24) and e2 (WSJ range, Aug. 1); reported alongside continuing administration figures well above this range, underscoring the persistent gap between administration and tracker figures.

estimates.tracker: Goldman Sachs (analysts Daan Struyven and Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby)
estimates.note: Crude AND refined products: 'Total exports of crude and oil products passing through the waterway have risen to 15 million to 16 million barrels a day' — a different quantity than the crude-only figures in this dispute, so it never enters the crude episode. Implied pre-war base ~23; March trough 5-6; note credits rising dark crossings and ship-to-ship transfers. Some aggregator rewrites render the scope as region-wide; this row follows the Bloomberg text as syndicated.

Oil that left the Arabian Sea on 31 August, Hormuz transits and the UAE bypass through the Gulf of Oman together, per Fortune. A single-day volume for the whole region, so it never enters the rate episode.

A 28-day moving average to 31 August of crude and products together, attributed to Vortexa senior analyst Rohit Rathod; a 28-day average is not one of this ledger's periods. All liquids, so out of the crude episode. The Axios page could not be reopened on 19 October; the Monday monitor read it on 7 and 14 September and recorded the same figure both times.
The same series for 1 September, the day of Wright's 'more than 17 million barrels' (archive USOF-20260901-01). The two cover different water by different methods, so they are not compared.

'Kpler said crude exports excluding Iran had also recovered to at least 16.5 million bpd as an average over September', published 5 October; the post-month reading of the series whose preliminary value was 16.3 (e10). Stated as a floor, so no upper value.

September average, published 6 October: 'combined crude and condensate exports from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar and Iran rose to about 14.7 million bpd in September from 10.8 million bpd in August'. Seven countries including Iran, by all routes; a different basis from Kpler's Middle East tally in e10 to e15.

September average, published 6 October: 'Flows of crude, condensate and refined fuels including LPG averaged 19.2 million barrels per day', Gulf exports excluding Iran by all routes, 81 percent of the pre-war rate.

'Hormuz oil exports averaging just under 9 million barrels a day in September, about 44 per cent of pre-war levels', published 12 October beside Wright's 80 to 90 percent. Stated as a ceiling, so no lower or central value. A later and higher reading of September than e11 (6.5, September to 21 September); the two sit side by side.

Seven-day average of oil leaving the Arabian Sea to 2 September. The same report gives a 28-day average of 6.85, not entered because a 28-day average is not one of this ledger's periods. Regional, so out of the Hormuz episode; e6 is the firm's 28-day Hormuz-only average of 5.04 from the same days.
The same series for 2 September. Fortune says the daily volumes swing far more than before the war.

Average over the previous 28 days of oil leaving through the Strait itself; a further 2.49 mb/d left from Gulf of Oman terminals, 7.54 mb/d in total across the U.S. Navy line against 17.67 in January and February. The firm's post says 'oil' and only later 'crude oil'; a 28-day average is not one of this ledger's periods.

'During the war, daily observed oil and product exit volumes have ranged mostly between 4 million and 6 million barrels per day': the band of daily readings over the war to date, not one week. Oil plus products, so it never enters the crude episode.

'Exports through Hormuz have reached around 6.5 million barrels per day so far in September, the highest since the brief spike after the June ceasefire': a September-to-date average as of 21 September; the column does not say crude or all liquids. Kpler also expected about 2.5 mb/d of crude to load by ship-to-ship transfer in the Gulf of Oman in September.

'Kpler data showed crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to 19.5-22.5 million bpd': the range spans four single days, dated here to the last. Pre-war average 18 mb/d. Middle East crude by all routes, including the Red Sea, terminals and Gulf of Oman transfers.

'Flows through the Strait of Hormuz were projected to reach about 9.7 million barrels a day as Saudi Arabia sent additional crude from its Gulf terminals after attacks damaged its East-West pipeline': a September projection, the Hormuz part of Kpler's crude export tally, though the sentence says 'flows'.

'Preliminary data from Kpler put regional exports at 16.3 million barrels a day' for September, the highest month since the war began and about 3.2 mb/d below February's 19.5. Middle East crude by all routes.

'The overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30.' Middle East exports by all routes; all liquids, so it never enters the crude episode.

'The seven-day moving average for Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared with an average of about 18 million bpd during the 12 months before the war.' Regional, all routes; the same series as e15 one day earlier.

'On October 1, the seven-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd'; the figure includes transits through Hormuz, the Red Sea, terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Pre-war average 18 mb/d.

Kpler's own post: 'combined crude volumes exiting the Gulf (excluding Iran) plus volumes from West Coast Saudi and East Coast UAE are around pre-conflict levels of 18.5 Mbd' and 'now around 100%'. No averaging window given. Clean product loadings are given separately at 2.5 to 3 mb/d, about half of pre-war.
'The 14-day moving average for Middle East crude and condensate exports had reached 18.6 million bpd': a 14-day average, not one of this ledger's periods, dated to the article. Regional, all routes.
'Shipments from the Middle East as a whole stood at 15.3 million bpd, 10% below prewar levels': the same Kpler week as e32. Regional, so out of the Hormuz episode.

'Exports through Hormuz stood at 8.5 million barrels a day (bpd) for the week ended Wednesday, about 40% below normal before the war, according to Kpler data published Friday': the week to 7 October, published 9 October. The week after e21's floor of 10.1; the fall came as attacks on tankers in and around the strait reached a wartime weekly high.

'Crude crossing the strait fell 27% from a wartime high the week before, to at least 10.1 million barrels a day', which Kpler says is back to its September average but 74 percent of its pre-war level. A weekly figure for the week before 8 October; stated as a floor, so no upper value.

The high day of the same single-day series as e24, given in the same report. Sits beside e21, Kpler's weekly floor of 10.1 million barrels a day for the week before 8 October, which is a different measure.

'About 20.8 million barrels passed through on 8 October but only 2.9 million on 11 October': the lowest single day of the month to that point. A single-day volume, so it never enters the rate episode.

'In the week to October 13, the daily average dropped to 11.62 million barrels, from a baseline of 17.15 million barrels daily'; Al Jazeera's account of the same figure gives 11.6 against 17.1, about 68 percent of pre-war. Kpler analysts put the fall down to heavier Iranian attacks on tankers and expect a slower, more uneven recovery without a political settlement. The column says 'oil flows', not crude or all liquids.

'Crude exports through Hormuz have pulled back after touching prewar levels in September. Shipments stood at 9.4 million barrels per day for the week ended Wednesday, about 70% of the average before the Iran war': the week to 14 October, published 16 October. The newest reading in the episode, a day after e23's 11.62 for the seven days to 13 October; the windows differ by a day and daily flows swing widely, so this is a later reading, not a correction.

scope_definitions.hormuz_outbound: Oil claimed or estimated to be exiting through the Strait of Hormuz itself.
scope_definitions.regional_total_including_bypass: Hormuz flow plus bypass pipelines and export routes; not comparable to Hormuz-only figures.
scope_definitions.ship_transits_in_and_out: Vessel transits counted in both directions; includes empty inbound ships, so not a loaded-outbound count.

method.gap: The verification gap is the claimed flow minus the independent tracker consensus, computed only within one scope, one unit, and one time window. It is labeled unverified, not false.
method.estimates_provenance: Independent tracker figures reach this dataset secondhand, as reported by the named press outlet on each row.
method.resolution: The gap can only be resolved retrospectively: Gulf loadings, destination arrivals and official trade data. First referee: official Iraq/Kuwait/Saudi export figures for August 2026, expected around October-November 2026, already tracked by this site's official-tally instrument.
method.dark_transits: Ships operating without AIS may explain part of the gap (a tracker undercount). A missed VLCC is roughly 2 million barrels. The explanation cuts both ways and is not adjudicated here.

guardrails: The difference is labeled unverified, never lying or exaggeration.
Comparisons never cross scopes or units.
Anonymous attributions are marked as such.
PortWatch activity indices are never converted into barrels-per-day estimates.
Every value carries a dated, linked source.
